title: Accounting for Share Capital
summary: A company raises its owned funds by issuing shares. This chapter covers features and kinds of companies, types of shares and share capital, issue of shares at par and at premium, over- and under-subscription, calls in arrears and in advance, issue for consideration other than cash, private placement, ESOP, forfeiture and reissue of shares, and disclosure of share capital under Schedule III of the Companies Act, 2013.

notes.heading: Company: meaning, features and kinds
notes.html:
A company is an artificial person created by law, with a separate legal entity, perpetual succession and limited liability [Section 2(20), Companies Act, 2013].

  • Separate legal entity: it can own property, sue and be sued in its own name.
  • Limited liability: shareholders' liability is limited to the unpaid amount on their shares.
  • Perpetual succession: existence is not affected by death or change of members.
  • Transferability of shares: shares of a public company are freely transferable.
  • Separation of ownership and management: managed by elected directors.
  • Common seal: optional under the 2013 Act; documents may be authenticated by authorised signatories.

Kinds: on the basis of liability — limited by shares, limited by guarantee, unlimited; on the basis of members — private company (minimum 2, maximum 200 members), public company (minimum 7, no maximum), One Person Company (single member); others — government company, holding and subsidiary company, listed company.

notes.heading: Shares and categories of share capital
notes.html:
Under Section 43, share capital is of two kinds:

  • Preference shares: carry a preferential right to dividend at a fixed rate and to return of capital on winding up. They may be cumulative or non-cumulative, participating or non-participating, convertible or non-convertible, redeemable (irredeemable preference shares cannot be issued).
  • Equity shares: all shares that are not preference shares; they carry voting rights and bear the highest risk.
CategoryMeaning
Authorised capitalMaximum capital the company is authorised to raise by its Memorandum (also called nominal or registered capital)
Issued capitalPart of authorised capital offered to the public (and others) for subscription
Subscribed capitalPart of issued capital actually taken up; shown as 'subscribed and fully paid' and 'subscribed but not fully paid'
Called-up capitalPart of subscribed capital the company has asked shareholders to pay
Paid-up capitalPart of called-up capital actually received = Called-up capital − Calls in arrears
Uncalled capitalSubscribed capital not yet called
Reserve capitalPart of uncalled capital that the company decides by special resolution to call only on winding up (Section 65)

notes.heading: Key legal rules for issue of shares
notes.html:
• Application money: not less than 5% of the nominal value (Section 39); SEBI requires at least 25% of the issue price for public issues by listed companies.
  • Minimum subscription: 90% of the issue must be subscribed; otherwise the entire application money is refunded within the time limit fixed by law and SEBI.
  • Issue at premium (Section 52): premium is credited to Securities Premium, which can be used only for: (i) issuing fully paid bonus shares; (ii) writing off preliminary expenses; (iii) writing off expenses of, commission paid or discount allowed on issue of securities; (iv) premium payable on redemption of preference shares or debentures; (v) buy-back of own shares (Section 68).
  • Issue at discount (Section 53): prohibited, except sweat equity shares issued to employees or directors under Section 54.
  • Private placement (Section 42): offer of securities to a select group of persons (not more than 200 in a financial year, excluding qualified institutional buyers and employees under ESOP) through a private placement offer letter.
  • ESOP: an option given to employees and directors to buy the company's shares at a future date at a pre-determined price, usually lower than the market price.

notes.heading: Over-subscription and pro-rata allotment: worked illustration 1
notes.html:
When applications exceed shares offered, directors may (a) reject excess applications and refund, (b) allot pro rata and adjust excess money towards allotment/calls, or (c) combine both.

XYZ Ltd issued 50,000 equity shares of ₹10 each at a premium of ₹2, payable: application ₹3, allotment ₹5 (including premium ₹2), first and final call ₹4. Applications were received for 70,000 shares: applications for 10,000 shares were rejected and refunded; applicants for 60,000 shares were allotted 50,000 shares pro rata (6:5), excess money being adjusted on allotment. Ram, holding 500 shares, paid allotment but not the call; his shares were forfeited and later reissued at ₹8 per share fully paid.

notes.heading: Forfeiture and reissue of shares
notes.html:
Forfeiture is cancellation of shares for non-payment of allotment or call money, as per the Articles. Entry on forfeiture:

Share Capital A/c Dr (called-up amount per share x number of shares)
Securities Premium A/c Dr (only if premium was not received)
To Unpaid Allotment/Calls A/c (or Calls in Arrears A/c)
To Share Forfeiture A/c (amount received, excluding premium received)

Reissue: forfeited shares may be reissued at par, premium or discount. The discount on reissue cannot exceed the amount forfeited on those shares; it is debited to Share Forfeiture A/c. Premium on reissue is credited to Securities Premium A/c.

After reissue, the balance in Share Forfeiture A/c relating to reissued shares is a capital profit and is transferred to Capital Reserve. The balance relating to shares not yet reissued stays in Share Forfeiture A/c and is added to paid-up capital in the balance sheet.

Worked illustration 2: premium not received

notes.heading: Disclosure of share capital in the balance sheet
notes.html:
Share capital appears under Equity and Liabilities → Shareholders' Funds → (a) Share Capital, with details in the Notes to Accounts. Securities Premium and Capital Reserve appear under (b) Reserves and Surplus. Calls in advance appear under Other Current Liabilities.

notes.heading: Common mistakes to avoid
notes.html:
• Debiting Securities Premium on forfeiture even though the premium was received.
  • Crediting the entire forfeited amount to Capital Reserve when only part of the shares is reissued.
  • Allowing a discount on reissue larger than the forfeited amount.
  • Forgetting that pro-rata excess money reduces the cash received on allotment.
  • Showing calls in arrears as a current asset; it is deducted from subscribed capital in the note.
  • Showing share forfeiture under Reserves and Surplus; it is added to share capital.

keyTerms.definition: A unit into which the total share capital of a company is divided.
Share that is not a preference share; carries voting rights and residual claim on profits and assets.
Share with preferential right to a fixed dividend and to repayment of capital on winding up.
Maximum capital a company can raise as stated in its Memorandum of Association.
Excess of issue price over face value of shares; its use is restricted by Section 52.
Amount called up but not paid by shareholders on the due date.
Amount received from shareholders before it is called; a current liability.
Allotment of shares in a fixed proportion to the number of shares applied for, in case of over-subscription.
Cancellation of shares for non-payment of allotment or call money; amount already received is forfeited.
Sale of forfeited shares again, at par, premium or a discount not exceeding the forfeited amount.
Issue of securities to a select group of persons (not more than 200 in a year, excluding QIBs and ESOP employees) under Section 42.
Option given to employees and directors to buy company shares at a future date at a pre-determined, usually lower, price.

formulas.name: Excess application money (pro-rata)
formulas.html: (Shares applied by pro-rata applicants − Shares allotted) x Application money per share

formulas.name: Amount forfeited
formulas.html: Amount received on forfeited shares towards capital (excluding premium received)

formulas.name: Share capital debited on forfeiture
formulas.html: Number of shares forfeited x Called-up value per share

formulas.name: Maximum discount on reissue
formulas.html: Amount forfeited on the shares being reissued

formulas.name: Capital reserve on reissue
formulas.html: Forfeited amount on reissued shares − Discount allowed on reissue

formulas.name: Number of shares for consideration other than cash
formulas.html: Amount payable to vendor / Issue price per share

mcqs.q: Securities Premium CANNOT be used for:
options: Issue of fully paid bonus shares
Writing off preliminary expenses
Payment of dividend
Premium payable on redemption of debentures
mcqs.explanation: Section 52 lists permitted uses; paying dividend is not one of them, as premium is a capital receipt.

mcqs.q: Under the Companies Act, 2013, shares cannot be issued at a discount except:
options: Bonus shares
Sweat equity shares
Right shares
Preference shares
mcqs.explanation: Section 53 prohibits issue at discount, but sweat equity shares under Section 54 are an exception.

mcqs.q: A company cannot allot shares unless the minimum subscription of the issue received is:
mcqs.explanation: Minimum subscription is 90% of the issue; otherwise application money must be refunded.

mcqs.q: 300 shares of ₹10 each, issued at par, were forfeited. ₹7 per share had been called up and the shareholder had paid ₹4 per share. The amount credited to Share Forfeiture A/c is:
mcqs.explanation: Amount received = 300 x 4 = ₹1,200, which is forfeited.

mcqs.q:
Assertion (A): The balance in Share Forfeiture Account relating to reissued shares is transferred to Capital Reserve.
Reason (R): It is a capital profit that cannot be distributed as dividend.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
mcqs.explanation: The surplus is a gain of a capital nature, so it goes to Capital Reserve; R explains A.

mcqs.q: Case: A company invited applications for 80,000 shares, application money ₹2 per share. Applications were received for 1,20,000 shares and all applicants were allotted shares pro rata. The excess application money to be adjusted on allotment is:
100 forfeited shares of ₹10 each (forfeited amount ₹600) were reissued at ₹8 per share fully paid. The amount transferred to Capital Reserve is:
mcqs.explanation: Discount on reissue = 100 x 2 = ₹200; capital reserve = 600 − 200 = ₹400.

mcqs.q: Calls in arrears are shown in the balance sheet of a company:
options: Under other current liabilities
Under other current assets
As a deduction from 'subscribed but not fully paid' capital in the note on share capital
As an addition to share capital
mcqs.explanation: Paid-up capital = called-up capital minus calls in arrears, shown in the note on share capital.

mcqs.q:
Assertion (A): A public company can issue its equity shares to the public at a discount.
Reason (R): Section 53 of the Companies Act, 2013 prohibits issue of shares at a discount except sweat equity shares.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
mcqs.explanation: Because of Section 53, A is false; R correctly states the law.

mcqs.q: A company purchased assets worth ₹5,50,000 and paid by issuing equity shares of ₹10 each at a premium of 10%. The number of shares issued is:
200 shares of ₹10 each, on which ₹6 per share had been paid, were forfeited. The maximum total discount at which they can be reissued is:
mcqs.explanation: Discount on reissue cannot exceed the forfeited amount: 200 x 6 = ₹1,200.

mcqs.q: Case: 200 shares of ₹10 each were issued at ₹12; ₹3 was payable on application and ₹5 (including premium ₹2) on allotment. A holder paid only the application money and his shares were forfeited after allotment. The amount credited to Share Forfeiture A/c is:
mcqs.explanation: Only application money of 200 x 3 = ₹600 was received; premium was not received, so Securities Premium is debited ₹400 and Share Capital ₹1,200.

questions.q: What is meant by 'subscribed but not fully paid' capital?
questions.answerHtml: It is that part of subscribed capital on which the full nominal value has not yet been called or received, i.e. some calls are yet to be made or are in arrears.

questions.q: Under which head and sub-head is Securities Premium shown in the balance sheet of a company?
questions.answerHtml: Head: Shareholders' Funds; sub-head: Reserves and Surplus.

questions.q: State any three purposes for which Securities Premium can be used under Section 52 of the Companies Act, 2013.
questions.answerHtml:
1. Issuing fully paid bonus shares to members.
  2. Writing off preliminary expenses of the company.
  3. Writing off expenses of, commission paid or discount allowed on issue of shares or debentures.

(Also: premium payable on redemption of preference shares or debentures; buy-back of its own shares under Section 68.)
